newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss National Bank sees no urgent need to tighten.
newsitem.headline: Swiss National Bank sees no urgent need to tighten.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) sees no reason to push interest rates higher now due to the country's weak economy, but will not let loose monetary policy drive inflation higher, its chief economist said.
"In view of the continued tendency towards stagnation, there's no pressing need so far for a tighter monetary policy," Georg Rich said in the text of a speech to be delivered here.
But he also said that while monetary policy can lay the groundwork for a recovery, it is not a panacea for economic ills which are structural in nature.
"Monetary policy creates the prerequisites for the expected economic recovery. But it is no elixir to be used to cure economic stagnation," he said.

"It cannot be used as a substitute for urgently needed measures to strengthen Switzerland's competitiveness as a place to do business. It is an illusion to believe that with an expansive monetary policy you can delay structural changes taking place in Switzerland and other countries," he said.
"It is hardly possible to hold production and employment perfectly stable without endangering price stability," he said.

"The occasional demand that the National Bank should pay more attention to unemployment is misdirected. If it tried to reduce unemployment significantly, it would have to take into account a significant rise in inflation," Rich said.

The Swiss franc level plays a part in SNB policy, he said, refering to a period when the Swiss franc was seen as overvalued. He did not say whether, after recent weakening, the franc has fallen far enough.
But, recalling past foreign exchange rate movements, he said the SNB could not afford to lose sight of the long-term implications Swiss franc fluctuations pose for price stability.

"Some of our critics are of the opinion that we could have avoided the sharp rise in the franc if we had conducted monetary policy in a manner aimed at stabilising the exchange rate," Rich said. But, he added: "Greater emphasis on the exchange rate would have created new problems."

The Swiss franc has fallen sharply in recent months. It traded at roughly three-year lows against the dollar on Monday, as the U.S. unit rose over 1.47 francs. The franc's decline, in part due to a more expansive SNB policy, is aimed at boosting Swiss exports.

"We of course are aware of the pain which results from a too-strong franc rate. For that reason, the exchange rate is part of our monetary policy calculations. But we cannot lose sight of medium- and long-term impact of our measures. A stronger focus on the franc would have forced us to open the money sluices," Rich said.

"We would not only have deflationary pressure in the Swiss economy. We would have summoned up danger of a renewed inflationary upswing," Rich said. "We could not and did not want to take this risk," he added. (( -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340))
